title: Masquerading: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location
shortTitle: Masquerading: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location
summary: Matching a legitimate resource name or location means placing a malicious file, registry key or container object where its name and path are already associated with something trusted. Typical forms are an unsigned executable dropped into a system directory, a payload named after a well-known Windows process, and a registry key whose name is a close approximation of one written by legitimate software, including subtle spelling changes and trailing spaces. The technique works because analysts and detection logic often whitelist by path or name, so the object inherits trust it never earned. Detection relies on volume and content comparisons rather than on the string itself: a file whose name matches a system binary but whose hash, signature, version resource or creation time does not match the vendor baseline, duplicates of a system binary outside their expected path, and registry keys under vendor branches that no installer in the software inventory created. In containerised environments the same logic applies to namespaces, pod names and image tags that imitate platform components, so the useful check is whether the object was created by the platform or by something else.

beginner.definition: This is when an attacker gives their file a trusted name or drops it in a trusted folder. The name or place makes it look normal. A system folder on Windows is a common target. So is a registry key, which is a settings store for the system.
beginner.whyItMatters: People and tools often trust a file because of its name or its location. That trust can be borrowed by anyone who can write to the same folder. A file called like a system program may never be checked. Attackers also use similar looking names to fool a quick reading of a list.
howItWorks: The attacker copies their program into a folder the system normally trusts.
They name it after an existing system program so it blends into the listing.
Sometimes they use a near miss name with a small spelling change.
The file is then run by a user, a script or another program.
They can do the same with registry keys, using names close to real vendor keys.
In cloud and container systems they copy trusted namespaces and object names.
beginner.example: Picture a hospital night desk where staff trust anyone wearing a ward uniform. A visitor finds a spare uniform in a cupboard and puts it on. They now walk past the desk without a question. Nobody checked who they were.
takeaways: A trusted folder is not proof that a file belongs there.
Typo and near miss names are a common way to borrow trust.
Compare file hashes, signatures and creation times against a baseline.

objectives: Explain how a file or registry key can borrow trust from its name or location.
List common locations attackers use to place payloads that look legitimate.
Describe how near miss names defeat review by eye.
Identify artefacts that separate a real system file from a planted copy.
Recognise the same behaviour in container namespaces and object names.
